lines.text: ${name} is surrounded. Supply lines are cut, morale is fracturing, and ${topNPCName}, the ${topNPCRole}, is deciding whether to negotiate terms or hold out for relief that may not be coming.
The siege has entered its second week; ${govFaction} controls the rationing and the gates, which means they control everything else too, for now.
Every ${commodity} cache in ${name} has been inventoried and argued over; the next argument will be about what to give up and what to defend to the end.

The walls of ${name} have held so far, which is the problem. A quick fall would at least have settled the question of who was to blame, and a slow one leaves ${govFaction} to answer for every day the relief does not come.
${name} is learning the arithmetic of a siege: how many mouths, how many days of ${commodity}, how many of the people on the walls are watching the enemy and how many are watching each other.
Word came into ${name} three days ago that the relief column had turned back; ${topNPCName}, the ${topNPCRole}, has not made it public, and the effort of not making it public is beginning to show.

lines.text: ${name} is two bad weeks from genuine starvation; ${topFaction} controls the remaining ${commodity} reserves and is not discussing it openly.
The harvest failure has restructured every relationship in ${name}. Whoever controls food now controls the settlement, and at least three factions have worked this out.
${topNPCName}, the ${topNPCRole}, knows where the hoarded ${commodity} can be found, and isn't saying, and the reasons for that silence are complicated.
The bakers of ${name} have started cutting the bread with things that are not flour; everyone can taste it, and the fact that nobody complains is the most alarming part.
${govFaction} of ${name} announced a fair distribution of the ${commodity} reserves last week; the announcement and the distribution are turning out to be two different things.
Hunger has made ${name} quiet. The market still opens, the queues still form, but the haggling has gone out of people. They take what they are given and calculate, silently, how long it will last.

lines.text: ${name} is under occupation; ${govFaction} answers to outside authority now, which means every decision made here is made twice: once officially, once actually.

The occupation has been running long enough that some residents have accommodated it and some have organised against it, and the divide between those two groups is not always visible from the outside.
${topNPCName}, the ${topNPCRole}, is simultaneously expected to enforce the occupiers' directives and protect the people those directives are aimed at: a position that is becoming untenable.
The occupiers of ${name} are careful to leave the forms of local rule in place (${govFaction} still meets, still signs, still presides) which fools no one and is not meant to.
Every household in ${name} has quietly decided what it would and would not do if asked, and most of them are hoping never to find out whether they were honest with themselves.
The curfew in ${name} is enforced unevenly, and the unevenness is the point: no one can be sure which night, or which street, or which face at the checkpoint will decide that the rules apply to them.

lines.text: ${name} has no effective government; ${topFaction} controls one district and the institutions inside it, a rival controls another, and the contested space between them is where things go wrong.
Three factions are each waiting for one of the other two to make a mistake. In the meantime, ${name} is being administered by inertia.
${topNPCName}, the ${topNPCRole}, is the only person all three factions will still speak to, which makes them either the key to resolution or the next target.

Nothing gets decided in ${name} because deciding would require one faction to be seen to win, and none of them can afford to let another be seen to lose. The paralysis is not an accident; it is the only stable arrangement left.

${name} runs two of everything now (two watches, two courts of a kind, two versions of who is owed what), and the citizens have learned which one to approach for which favour, which is its own kind of government.
The last thing ${topFaction} and its rivals agreed on in ${name} was that the disagreement should not be allowed to reach the streets; that agreement is the only thing holding, and it is fraying.

lines.text: ${name} owes more than it can repay; the creditor's representative arrived last month, and every civic decision since has been made with one eye on what they might accept as partial satisfaction.
${topFaction} took the loans and ${govFaction} is repaying them: a distinction that has not gone unnoticed and is not forgotten.
The debt has a clause that ${topNPCName} has read and that would change the entire conversation if it became public.
The creditor has begun taking payment from ${name} in things other than coin (a warehouse here, a toll right there), and each transfer is legal, documented, and slightly worse than the last.

${name} still keeps up appearances: the civic buildings are painted, the festival was held. The money for both was borrowed, which everyone knows and no one says, because saying it would end the appearances that are the only asset left.
The interest on ${name}'s debt now outpaces what the ${commodity} can bring in; the numbers have been quietly rearranged twice to hide it, and there is no third arrangement that works.

lines.text: Someone inside ${name} sold something important (recently enough that the wound is open, not yet scarred over), and the settlement's institutions are running at reduced trust while everyone suspects everyone else.
The betrayal's consequences are still unfolding; ${topNPCName}, the ${topNPCRole}, knows more than they've disclosed about what was sold and to whom.
${govFaction} has been investigating the betrayal for three weeks with nothing to show for it, which either means they're incompetent or the answer leads somewhere they don't want to go.
Since the betrayal, ${name} has become a place where people finish fewer sentences and lock more doors; the trust that made the settlement work is not gone, but it is being rationed.
Everyone in ${name} has privately assembled their own list of who might have done it, and the lists do not agree, and the disagreement is doing almost as much damage as the original act.

The betrayal cost ${name} something specific (a contract, a caravan, a name that vouched for the place), and the loss of it is only now working its way through the ledgers, arriving as bad news that seems, wrongly, unrelated.

lines.text: ${name} doesn't know it's been infiltrated; decisions at the ${govFaction} level have been subtly shaped for months, and the direction those decisions have been shaped toward is only now becoming legible.
Someone has been in ${name} long enough to understand it (its vulnerabilities, its factions, its trusted figures), and has been using that understanding systematically.
Three separate things have gone slightly wrong in ${name} recently, in ways that look like bad luck; they are not bad luck.

The infiltration of ${name} shows only in negatives: the meeting that was rescheduled at exactly the wrong moment, the shipment that was delayed just long enough, the appointment that went to the second-best candidate for reasons no one can quite reconstruct.

Whoever is inside ${name} has not asked for anything yet, and the waiting is the tell: they are still building the position, and by the time they spend it, it will be too late for ${govFaction} to have noticed.

${topNPCName}, the ${topNPCRole}, has become, without anyone deciding it, the person through whom a surprising amount of ${name}'s sensitive business now passes, which is either coincidence or the whole design.

lines.text: Something is spreading in ${name}; the quarantine is partial, the healers are overwhelmed, and the ${topNPCRole} who first identified it has gone quiet in a way that suggests either pressure or something worse.
The disease has not yet become a plague, but the window for preventing that outcome is narrowing; every day the quarantine is ignored or negotiated around makes the arithmetic worse.
${govFaction} is managing disclosure of the outbreak, which means what residents know and what is actually true have started to diverge.

The sickness in ${name} has already sorted the population into those who can afford to leave, those who can afford to isolate, and those who can do neither, and the last group has noticed the sorting.
The healers of ${name} have stopped arguing about what the illness is and started arguing about what to do with the bodies, which is the point at which denial stops being an option for anyone.

A cordon has gone up around one quarter of ${name}, and the people inside it and the people outside it are already telling different stories about why: stories that will outlast the sickness whichever way it goes.

lines.text: ${name} has no effective leader; the last strong authority died ${weeksAgo} weeks ago, and ${topFaction} is moving faster than the settlement's institutions can process what's happening.
Three different people in ${name} believe they should be in charge; two of them are wrong; none of them is certain; all of them are acting.
The power vacuum is obvious to everyone; the question is not who fills it but what they do to fill it and who they owe when they have.

The old authority in ${name} left no clear heir and a great many people who benefited from the old arrangement; each of them is now discovering that a claim is only as good as the people willing to enforce it.

${name} is being run, for the moment, by whoever holds the keys, the seals, and the granary: three things that used to be held by one office and are now held by three people who do not trust one another.

The succession in ${name} will be settled by the ${commodity} more than by any claim of blood or law: whoever the merchants and the creditors decide to deal with becomes, retroactively, the legitimate successor.

lines.text: The attacks on ${name}'s outlying farmsteads are following a pattern that doesn't fit opportunistic predation; someone or something is directing this, and the evidence is available to anyone who looks carefully.
The settlement's defences are adequate for normal times; these are not normal times, and ${topNPCName}, the ${topNPCRole}, knows it.
Three farmsteads have been abandoned in the last month; the families who abandoned them know something about what they saw that they haven't reported to the authorities.
${name} has drawn its edges inward (fields left unworked, a mill standing idle) trading the ${commodity} it needs for a perimeter ${milForce} can actually hold.

The bounty ${govFaction} posted for the creature has attracted the wrong sort of help to ${name}: hunters who are more dangerous than useful, and who will expect payment whether or not the thing is dead.

Whatever is preying on ${name} has learned the settlement's patterns (when the patrols pass, where the walls are thin) which is not something a beast does, and admitting that is the first hard conversation no one wants to open.

lines.text: The commons of ${name} have stopped pretending to accept the current arrangement. ${govFaction} still holds the buildings and the official seal, but it is governing by momentum rather than consent. The first faction leader to offer a credible alternative will find an audience.

The street has gone quiet in ${name}, and the quiet is not calm. It is the pause before a thing that everyone can feel coming. ${govFaction} issues orders that are heard, noted, and not obeyed, and each unobeyed order costs it more than the last.

In ${name} the rents go uncollected, the summons go unanswered, and the men ${govFaction} sends to enforce either turn back or turn coat. The revolt has not started because it has, in every way that matters, already happened.

lines.text: The challenge to ${govFaction} in ${name} is institutional, not the street but the ledger and the meeting room. Revenue is being held. Officials are slow-walking decisions. Someone is building a coalition, and ${govFaction} knows it but cannot act without legitimising what they are trying to suppress.

The insurgency in ${name} wears a clerk's coat. Permits stall in the right offices, funds arrive short and late, and the people doing it can each point to a rule that excuses them. ${govFaction} is being strangled by its own procedures, wielded by people who have read them more carefully than it has.

No one in ${name} is marching, and that is what makes it dangerous. The opposition to ${govFaction} is a patient, well-lawyered thing that means to inherit the settlement intact rather than take it by force, and it is close to being able to.

lines.text: ${name} is absorbing more people than it was built for. The new arrivals and the old residents are not yet one community. They share streets and markets but not language, custom, or trust. ${govFaction} is managing the rate of change rather than directing it, and the rate of change is not cooperating.

The ${commodity} that made ${name} worth coming to cannot keep pace with the number who came. Housing is short, rents have doubled, and the newcomers who were welcomed as labour a year ago are being spoken of as a problem this one, though they have done nothing but arrive.

${name} has grown a second town at its edges. Newer, poorer, and not quite governed by the same rules as the first. ${govFaction} has not decided whether the outer town is part of the settlement or a thing that has happened to it, and the indecision is becoming a policy of its own.

lines.text: ${name} is taking in more people than it can feed. The newcomers came for work the town no longer has, and ${govFaction} is rationing what there is between families who have lived here for generations and families who arrived last month.
Every season brings more households to ${name} and no more work. The newcomers camp where they can, and ${govFaction} is counting heads it has no plan for.

The road into ${name} is busier than the road out, and both are watched. By ${govFaction}, which can neither turn people away nor keep them fed, and by the old residents, who are keeping a private account of who arrived.

lines.text: ${name} is at war and, for now, on the right side of it. Contracts are flowing, the garrison is reinforced, and the crown is paying. The men who left to fight have not come back, which is a grief that runs beneath the commerce. The question is whether the war ends before the accounts do.

The war has been good to ${name} so far, which is an uncomfortable thing to be. Being on the right side of it means the forges run day and night and the ${commodity} trade has never been dearer, and it means the settlement now needs the war to continue in order to pay for what the war has already cost it.

${name} is prospering on the right side of it: full warehouses, a reinforced garrison, coin moving fast. Prosperity built on a war is a wager that the war will end at the right moment, and no one in ${name} controls the moment.

lines.text: ${name} is losing people and resources to a war it did not choose the terms of. Conscription has hollowed out the skilled workforce. ${govFaction} signed a requisition order last week that it cannot afford and could not refuse. The settlement is loyal. It is also running thin.

The war reaches ${name} as a series of demands rather than battles: levies of men, of ${commodity}, of coin, each one framed as duty and none of them refusable. ${name} is losing people and resources it will not get back, and the front it is bleeding for is somewhere it will never see.

Every capable pair of hands ${name} could spare, and several it could not, has gone to the war; what remains is losing people and resources by attrition (a workshop closed for want of a master, a field unsown for want of a back) while ${govFaction} reports the settlement loyal and does not report the rest.

lines.text: The new faith in ${name} does not yet have a building. It has the congregation. ${govFaction} have not yet decided whether this is a religious matter, a political one, or both, and the delay in deciding is itself a decision that both sides are interpreting.

${name}'s religious community has formally split. Both factions hold services, keep records, and claim the legitimate succession. Every legal document that required religious sanction is now in a grey zone that the courts are not equipped to resolve quickly.

The conversion order in ${name} was formally acknowledged within the week. The compliance was faster than anyone expected. The depth of that compliance is a separate question that no one with authority is asking loudly, because the answer would require a response.

The new faith has taken the young of ${name} first, which the old faith has noticed and cannot answer. You cannot argue a congregation back, and every festival now draws two crowds of visibly different ages to two different squares.

${govFaction} in ${name} backed the winning faith a little too early and a little too visibly, and now find that a matter of belief has become a matter of who owes whom: the worst kind of debt to have taken on.

The conversion in ${name} is being managed as a property question as much as a spiritual one: which endowments, which burial rights, which festival days transfer with the congregation. The theology was settled quickly. The estate is where the fighting is.

lines.text: The revolt in ${name} is past the point where it could be resolved by show of force alone. The enslaved population controls enough territory and has enough organisation that suppression would require commitment the governing faction has not yet made. The market infrastructure that generated this situation is suspended. The question now is what the settlement looks like on the other side, and who decides.

${name} has stopped functioning as the thing it was. The labour it was built on has withdrawn itself, by force, and every calculation the settlement made about its own wealth turns out to have rested on people who are no longer willing to be a line in the ledger.

The rising in ${name} did not come from nowhere, though ${govFaction} is speaking of it as though it did. Everyone who is honest knows the grievances were real, old, and ignored, which makes the question of how to end it far harder than the question of how it began.

In ${name} the two sides have discovered they cannot simply win: the enslaved cannot hold the whole settlement, and ${govFaction} cannot retake it without destroying the ${commodity} that made it worth holding. What comes next will be a bargain neither wanted, struck between people who no longer pretend to be anything but enemies.
